questions.s: The median nerve
o: is found immediately lateral to the biceps tendon in the cubital fossa
From medial to lateral the fossa contains median nerve, brachial artery, biceps tendon. The nerve is medial to the artery, two structures medial to the tendon.
contains fibres from cervical roots 5, 6, 7 and 8 and thoracic 1
Last's: C5 to T1, from lateral (C5–7) and medial (C8, T1) roots.
is responsible for flexion of the distal interphalangeal joint of the little finger
The medial half of FDP (ring and little fingers) is supplied by the ulnar nerve.
is easily exposed in the arm where it is adjacent to the brachial artery by an incision along the medial border of biceps
It runs with the brachial artery along the medial bicipital groove, crossing from lateral to medial of it.

questions.s: Concerning the brachial plexus:
o: The divisions lie behind the clavicle at the outer border of the first rib
Roots and trunks are supraclavicular, the cords infraclavicular.
The cords are named by their relation to the second part of the axillary artery
They enter above the first part, embrace the second, and give branches around the third.
A prefixed plexus receives a major contribution from C4 and occurs in about 10%
Last's: prefixed (C4 to C8) and postfixed (C6 to T2) each occur in about 10%.
The lateral cord is formed by the anterior divisions of the middle and lower trunks
The lateral cord is formed by the anterior divisions of the upper and middle trunks. The medial cord is the anterior division of the lower trunk.

questions.s: Branches arising from the roots of the brachial plexus include the:
o: Suprascapular nerve
The suprascapular nerve arises from the upper trunk, the only trunk branch.
Dorsal scapular nerve
C5, passing behind the roots through scalenus medius.
Lateral pectoral nerve
It arises from the lateral cord.
Long thoracic nerve
C5, C6 and C7, passing behind the roots.

questions.s: Regarding the root values of branches of the brachial plexus:
o: Pectoralis major is the only muscle supplied by all five roots of the plexus
Last's: C5 and C6 to the clavicular head, C7, C8 and T1 to the sternocostal part.
The thoracodorsal nerve is C6, C7 and C8
It arises from the posterior cord and supplies latissimus dorsi.
The ulnar nerve receives its C7 fibres from the lateral cord in most people
Last's: in over 95% these come from the lateral cord, otherwise from the middle trunk. They supply FCU.
The axillary nerve is C7 and C8
The axillary nerve is C5 and C6.

questions.s: The long thoracic nerve:
o: Is formed by C5 and C6 roots passing through scalenus medius, joined by C7 which descends in front of the muscle
Last's description of its formation.
Runs down behind the midaxillary line on the surface of serratus anterior
So it lies behind the lateral cutaneous branches of the intercostal nerves and is safe from a midaxillary incision placed in front of it.
Supplies serratus anterior segmentally, with C7 to the lowest four digitations
C5 to the upper two, C6 to the next two, C7 to the lowest four.
Passes in front of the roots of the brachial plexus
The dorsal scapular and long thoracic nerves pass behind the roots. The nerve to subclavius passes in front of them.

questions.s: Concerning the axillary artery:
o: It is divided into three parts by pectoralis minor
First part above, second behind, third below.
The superior thoracic artery arises from the first part
One branch from the first part, two from the second, three from the third.
The lateral thoracic artery arises from the third part
The lateral thoracic and thoracoacromial arteries arise from the second part.
It becomes the brachial artery at the lower border of teres major
The axillary artery becomes the brachial artery at the lower border of teres major.

questions.s: Structures piercing the clavipectoral fascia include the:
o: Cephalic vein
Mnemonic CALL: cephalic vein, acromiothoracic (thoracoacromial) artery, lateral pectoral nerve, lymphatics.
Medial pectoral nerve
The medial pectoral nerve pierces pectoralis minor.
Lateral thoracic artery
It follows the lower border of pectoralis minor and does not pierce the clavipectoral fascia.
Long thoracic nerve
It runs on the surface of serratus anterior, nowhere near the fascia.

questions.s: Regarding the spaces of the posterior axillary wall:
o: The quadrangular space transmits the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral vessels
Bounded by teres minor above, teres major below, long head of triceps medially and the humerus laterally.
In the quadrangular space the axillary nerve lies below the vessels
Last's: the nerve lies above the vessels, in contact with the surgical neck just below the capsule.
The triangular space (interval) transmits the radial nerve and profunda brachii vessels
Bounded by teres major above, long head of triceps medially and the humerus laterally.
The circumflex scapular artery passes through the space bounded by teres minor, teres major and the long head of triceps
This is the upper triangular space, medial to the long head. The quadrangular space lies lateral to the long head.

questions.s: The axillary nerve:
o: Supplies teres major
Teres major is supplied by the lower subscapular nerve.
Supplies teres minor through its posterior branch
The posterior branch also supplies part of deltoid and becomes the upper lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm.
Supplies the skin of the back of the arm down to the elbow
That is the posterior cutaneous nerve of the arm (radial). The axillary nerve supplies skin over the lower half of deltoid.
Supplies the shoulder joint
It gives an articular branch.

questions.s: Concerning the musculocutaneous nerve:
o: It pierces coracobrachialis
It then slopes down between biceps and brachialis.
It supplies the lateral part of brachialis
It supplies the main part of brachialis. The lateral part, developed in the extensor compartment, is supplied by the radial nerve.
It becomes the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm lateral to the biceps tendon
It pierces the deep fascia at the elbow flexure crease.
Its root value is C5, C6 and C7
From the lateral cord.

questions.s: Within the cubital fossa:
o: The median nerve lies medial to the brachial artery
From medial to lateral: median nerve, brachial artery, biceps tendon.
The ulnar nerve lies medial to the median nerve
Last's: the ulnar nerve does not run in the cubital fossa. It passes behind the medial epicondyle.
The bicipital aponeurosis separates the median cubital vein from the brachial artery
It protects the artery and median nerve during venepuncture.
The radial nerve lies in the floor on supinator
The radial nerve lies just lateral to the fossa, in the slit between brachialis and brachioradialis.

questions.s: Regarding the median nerve:
o: It gives no muscular branches in the arm
Unless the branch to pronator teres arises unusually high.
It enters the forearm between the two heads of pronator teres
The ulnar head of pronator teres separates it from the ulnar artery.
Its palmar cutaneous branch passes deep to the flexor retinaculum
It arises just above the retinaculum and passes superficial to it, so it is spared in carpal tunnel syndrome.
It divides into its branches within the carpal tunnel
Last's: into lateral (with the muscular recurrent branch) and medial branches.

questions.s: The anterior interosseous nerve supplies:
o: Flexor pollicis longus
Deep flexor compartment muscles: FPL, lateral half of FDP and pronator quadratus.
The wrist and carpal joints
Last's: also the interosseous membrane and periosteum.
Pronator quadratus
It ends in this muscle.
The lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus
The part to the index and middle fingers.

questions.s: Concerning the flexor retinaculum and carpal tunnel:
o: The retinaculum is attached to the pisiform and hook of hamate medially
And to the tubercle of scaphoid and ridge of trapezium laterally.
The median nerve lies lateral to the tendons of FDS and medial to FCR
It lies just beneath the retinaculum, above FPL and FDP.
The ulnar nerve passes through the carpal tunnel
The ulnar nerve and artery pass superficial to the retinaculum, lateral to the pisiform.
Flexor pollicis brevis has the most variable nerve supply of any muscle
Last's: median recurrent branch, deep ulnar, or both.

questions.s: Regarding the ulnar nerve:
o: It gives no branches in the arm
True. The ulnar nerve gives no branches in the arm; its first branches are at the elbow. (Last's)
It pierces the medial intermuscular septum in the lower third of the arm
With the superior ulnar collateral artery and the radial nerve branch to medial head of triceps.
It enters the forearm between the two heads of flexor carpi ulnaris
Through the cubital tunnel.
It divides into superficial and deep branches proximal to the wrist crease
It divides on the flexor retinaculum, beside the pisiform. The dorsal branch arises proximal to the wrist.

questions.s: The deep branch of the ulnar nerve supplies:
o: Adductor pollicis
It ends there.
All the interossei
Palmar and dorsal.
The two medial lumbricals
Third and fourth.
The hypothenar muscles
The deep branch passes between flexor and abductor digiti minimi, through opponens digiti minimi, supplying all three.

questions.s: Concerning the radial nerve:
o: It gives a branch to the medial head of triceps in the axilla (the ulnar collateral nerve)
This runs with the ulnar nerve.
The posterior cutaneous nerve of the arm arises before the nerve enters the spiral groove
It supplies the back of the arm.
It enters the anterior compartment by piercing the lateral intermuscular septum
Then it lies between brachialis and brachioradialis.
It supplies extensor carpi radialis brevis before dividing
Last's: it supplies brachioradialis and ECRL, then gives the posterior interosseous nerve, which supplies ECRB and supinator.

questions.s: Following division of the superficial branch of the radial nerve at the wrist:
o: There is wrist drop
The superficial branch is purely sensory.
Sensory loss is often confined to a small area over the first dorsal interosseous
Last's: much overlap from the median and ulnar nerves.
There is weakness of extensor pollicis longus
EPL is supplied by the posterior interosseous nerve.
Sensory loss usually involves the anatomical snuffbox
Cutaneous branches cross the snuffbox tendons.

questions.s: The anatomical snuffbox:
o: Is bounded medially by extensor pollicis longus
And laterally by EPB and APL.
Has the scaphoid and trapezium in its floor
The radial styloid lies proximally.
Contains the radial artery
On the floor, deep to the tendons.
Contains the posterior interosseous nerve
The cephalic vein origin and branches of the superficial radial nerve lie here, not the PIN.

questions.s: Concerning the shoulder region muscles and nerves:
o: The suprascapular nerve passes below the superior transverse scapular ligament
The suprascapular vessels pass above it.
The suprascapular nerve supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus
C5 and C6 from the upper trunk.
Subscapularis is supplied by the upper and lower subscapular nerves
The lower also supplies teres major.
Teres minor is supplied by the suprascapular nerve
Teres minor is supplied by the axillary nerve.

questions.s: Regarding the segmental supply of upper limb movements:
o: Shoulder abduction and lateral rotation are C5
Adduction and medial rotation are C6 to C8.
Elbow flexion is C5 and C6
Elbow extension is C7 and C8.
Forearm pronation is C6
Supination is C6. Pronation is C7 and C8.
The intrinsic muscles of the hand are T1
Abductor pollicis brevis is a key T1 test.

questions.s: Regarding the upper limb dermatomes and axial lines:
o: The anterior axial line runs from the sternal angle down the front of the limb almost to the wrist
True. The anterior axial line runs from the sternal angle down the front of the limb almost to the wrist; there is no overlap across it. (Last's)
C7 supplies the middle finger
C6 the thumb (and probably index), C8 the ring and little fingers.
The posterior axial line runs from the vertebra prominens to the insertion of deltoid
True. The posterior axial line runs from the vertebra prominens across the back and down the arm to the deltoid insertion. (Last's)
T1 supplies the skin of the axilla
Last's: T1 supplies the medial side of the elbow region, not the axilla. T2 supplies the axilla.

questions.s: Following an upper trunk (C5, C6) brachial plexus injury:
o: The arm hangs medially rotated at the side
Loss of deltoid, supraspinatus, infraspinatus and teres minor gives the waiter's tip posture.
Elbow flexion is weak
Biceps, brachialis and brachioradialis are C5 and C6.
There is a sensory deficit over the lateral arm and forearm
C5 and C6 dermatomes.
The biceps jerk is preserved
The biceps jerk (C5, C6) is lost.

questions.s: A lower trunk (C8, T1) lesion with avulsion of the T1 root would produce:
o: Ipsilateral Horner's syndrome
Preganglionic sympathetic fibres to the head leave in the T1 root.
Wasting of the intrinsic hand muscles
T1 supplies the small muscles of the hand.
Sensory loss on the medial forearm
C8 and T1 territory.
Paralysis of deltoid
Deltoid is C5 and C6.

questions.s: Concerning arteries of the upper limb:
o: The subscapular artery continues as the thoracodorsal artery after giving the circumflex scapular
It runs down the posterior axillary wall.
The anterior and posterior circumflex humeral arteries arise from the third part of the axillary artery
With the subscapular.
The radial artery crosses the floor of the anatomical snuffbox
It then passes between the heads of the first dorsal interosseous.
The deep palmar arch is formed mainly by the ulnar artery
The deep arch is formed mainly by the radial artery. The superficial arch is mainly ulnar.

questions.s: Regarding ossification in the upper limb:
o: The clavicle is the first bone in the body to ossify
It ossifies in membrane from two centres in the fifth week.
The capitate is the first carpal bone to ossify
In the first year. Pisiform is last, at about 10 years.
The medial epicondyle of the humerus fuses with the shaft separately at about 20 years
The other three lower epiphyseal centres fuse together, then with the shaft at about 15 years.
The upper end of the radius is the growing end
The lower end is the growing end of the radius. In the upper limb the growing ends are at the shoulder and wrist.

questions.s: Concerning the posterior interosseous nerve:
o: It passes between the two layers of supinator
Under the arcade of Frohse.
It supplies all the muscles of the common extensor origin and the deep extensors
Including EPL, EPB, APL and extensor indicis.
It ends by supplying the wrist joint
It runs on the interosseous membrane.
It supplies brachioradialis
Brachioradialis is supplied by the radial nerve before its division.

questions.s: The recurrent (muscular) branch of the median nerve usually supplies:
o: Adductor pollicis
Adductor pollicis is supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve.
First dorsal interosseous
All interossei are supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve.
Palmaris brevis
Palmaris brevis is supplied by the superficial branch of the ulnar nerve.
Abductor pollicis brevis
The recurrent branch curves around the distal border of the retinaculum to the thenar muscles.

questions.s: Regarding the lumbricals and interossei:
o: The lumbricals arise from the tendons of flexor digitorum profundus
And insert into the radial side of the extensor expansions.
The lumbricals flex the metacarpophalangeal joints and extend the interphalangeal joints
Hence the claw deformity when they are paralysed.
The dorsal interossei adduct the fingers
Dorsal interossei abduct (DAB). Palmar interossei adduct (PAD).
The first and second lumbricals are usually supplied by the median nerve
The third and fourth by the deep ulnar nerve.
